title: The furniture store with a fountain show. And cookies.
summary: An afternoon with James in Reading: Fuddruckers, Jordan’s Liquid Fireworks, a Cookie Monstah dessert option and wheelchairs available near the entrance.
search: Out & about · Reading, Massachusetts The furniture store with a fountain show. And cookies. Fuddruckers, Jordan’s Furniture and Cookie Monstah: an afternoon with James in a place that turns out to be considerably more than a furniture store. A family field note · October 2026 · Reading, Massachusetts Lunch first. James at Fuddruckers in Reading, from our family camera roll. The little story ↓ The fountain show ↓ A simple plan ↓ Access & sensory notes ↓ Hours & links ↓ Some outings are planned in advance with tickets, schedules and an amount of preparation that could qualify as a second job. And then there is Jordan’s Furniture in Reading, where you can have lunch, watch illuminated fountains, browse a leather sofa and finish with cookies without getting back into the car. We began at Fuddruckers . There’s James in his navy shirt, sitting by the brick wall with that little smile I’m glad I caught. Sometimes the best photograph from a family outing is not in front of the attraction at all. It is the moment everyone has found a place to sit. For food decisions, we had a simple two-picture choice board showing grilled cheese with fries and macaroni and cheese with fries. The board is our own communication aid—not a claim that either dish is on the restaurant’s current menu. Having a familiar way to show a preference matters more to us than any elaborate printed menu. Fuddruckers also had a hand-spun milkshake board, with flavors from chocolate and vanilla to cookies and cream. No one needs to choose a shake to make lunch count, but the menu certainly made a good case for dessert. Our food-choice visual. It is a personal planning tool, not a verified restaurant menu. A little temptation on the Fuddruckers milkshake board. Prices and availability can change. And then the water began to dance. Jordan’s has a water-and-light display known as Liquid Fireworks . In our photographs, water arcs into the dark while green and violet light washes across the room. James is sitting nearby with a big tub of popcorn, looking toward the show. The photographs are some of my favorites from the afternoon. There was something pleasingly old-fashioned about it: a fountain show, a snack, the changing colors and time to watch as long as we wanted. Liquid Fireworks in Reading. Popcorn, fountains and an unexpectedly good stop. A family outing does not become better simply because you managed to fit in six more things. We did pause over the furniture, naturally. There was a beautiful tan leather sectional with a dark wood armrest and a clearance sign. If you find yourself comparing sofas halfway through a water show, that is simply the sort of place Jordan’s is. Cookie Monstah is also inside this same Reading location, so there’s a very appealing cookie-and-ice-cream stop to add if everyone still wants one. The shop is known for fresh-baked cookies and ice-cream cookie sandwiches. I like that this can be part of the afternoon rather than another drive, another parking lot and another set of transitions. We don’t need every part of a place to be suitable for us. The IMAX theater and ropes course are there for people who want them; the food, furniture and water display make a perfectly good smaller outing of their own. A close-up from the fountain show, with the popcorn firmly part of the experience. Yes, there was furniture, too. The very practical side of an otherwise surprising outing. The practical part A simple plan for another family. All three stops are at 50 Walkers Brook Drive, Reading, MA 01867 . You can make this a short visit or stretch it out, and you can decide on dessert after you know how the first part of the day is going. 1. Start with lunch. Use the Fuddruckers menu to plan the meal. If visual choices or AAC are helpful, bring familiar pictures, and check the actual options before offering the choice. 2. Watch the fountains. Find a position that gives everyone a view without needing to stay close to the sound and colored lights. Popcorn is optional. So is watching the whole show. 3. Leave dessert open. Cookie Monstah is right in the complex. A cookie, an ice-cream sandwich—or simply heading home—can all be perfectly good endings. Before you go Access, sound and the easy exit. Mobility A welcome practical detail from our visit: Jordan’s had wheelchairs available right by the entrance if you needed one. If you plan to borrow one, it is worth checking availability with the store before coming. Fuddruckers’ official Reading page lists wheelchair accessibility. Jordan’s IMAX information lists wheelchair spaces with companion seating, with an assisted entry route on request. Those theater details do not verify every route or attraction elsewhere in the building, so call ahead for individual access requirements. Sound & light The water-and-light display includes colored lighting and music, and the surrounding complex can be busy. Choose a viewing distance, bring preferred hearing protection if useful, and keep the option of stepping away. This is not an independently audited sensory-friendly venue. Food & communication Check up-to-date menus and allergen information directly. Familiar foods, visual options, AAC, a favorite snack or a short lunch can all help make an outing workable. Do not rely on our photograph of a temporary menu or posted price. Save this for later Where, hours and useful links. Jordan’s Furniture, Fuddruckers and Cookie Monstah 50 Walkers Brook Drive, Reading, Massachusetts 01867. Jordan’s currently lists store hours of Monday–Thursday 10–7, Friday–Saturday 10–8, and Sunday 11–6. Fuddruckers currently lists Monday–Thursday 11–7, Friday–Saturday 11–9, Sunday 11–6. Cookie Monstah and attraction hours may differ. Always check before setting out. title: Autumn, at Ruby’s pace.
summary: James, Ruby, and the simple joys of autumn—with a sensory nature guide for sitting, walking, or rolling, and outings across all six New England states.
search: The journal / Simple joys Autumn in New England · From the family album Autumn, at Ruby’s pace. James, a very busy yellow Lab, and the pleasure of an ordinary autumn visit with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve. October 14, 2026 · Family story & practical nature guide A little walk together ↓Plan your own time outside ↓ James and Ruby, with autumn underfoot. From our family camera roll. James has the leash and a wonderful grin. Ruby has her nose in the grass and apparently quite a lot to investigate. There are leaves scattered along the road, yellow beginning to show in the trees, and still enough warmth for shorts. A very New England sort of autumn. I love this photograph. James is looking up at the camera while Ruby gets on with the important business of being a dog. The leash makes a long white line between them. Around them, the season is quietly changing. Time with Mom-Mom & Grandpa Steve (aka Grandma & Grandpa) is part of what makes these ordinary days so dear. A visit, a little time outside, Ruby to walk, James right in the middle of it all. Being together can be as simple as that. Autumn in New England gives us so much to look at on an everyday walk. Green leaves hang on beside the gold ones. A few have already landed at the edge of the pavement. I like this part of the season, when summer is still showing up in somebody’s outfit and the trees have begun moving on. And then there is Ruby, who seems perfectly prepared to spend the afternoon examining one small patch of grass. She makes a good case for taking our time. There may be something very interesting by the next leaf. There is so much texture in this picture: the rough edge of the road, the soft-looking grass, Ruby’s pale coat against the dark pavement. It makes me think about how many ways there are to meet a season. Looking is one. Listening, feeling the air, or simply spending a few minutes in a familiar place are others. Nobody needs to notice the same thing. What I want for James is room to be part of the day in his own way. A lovely afternoon does not need a mileage goal, a completed activity, or a photograph in which everybody faces the camera. It can have pauses. It can change direction. It can end while there is still something left to see. These are the family photographs I want to keep coming back to: James smiling, Ruby nearby, the people we love woven into the day. Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve are part of that familiar, lovely world. A little walk together belongs in the family album just as much as a holiday or a birthday. A dog, some leaves, and time with the grandparents. The simple joys of autumn, right here. And if this photograph makes you want a little autumn of your own, here are some ways to begin. A bench, a smooth path, a garden, a window overlooking a tree: there is more than one good way outside. The practical field guide · New EnglandA little nature, your way.A sensory walk can be a sit, a roll, or a few minutes at the doorstep. Choose what feels interesting and comfortable today; every suggestion is optional. Choose your paceExplore the sensesFind a placeBefore you go 01 · Make room for everyoneChoose the outing that fits today. Universal design starts with choices built into the plan: a usable route, somewhere to rest, information in more than one form, and an easy way to finish. These ideas are for children, teens, and adults, with and without disabilities. Choose by preferences and support needs, not an ability ranking. Stay in one lovely spotTry five minutes beside a tree, at a garden table, or on an accessible viewing deck. A seated companion can share the same view. On a home day, watch branches from a window or enjoy a familiar nature photograph together. Go a little way & returnPick a firm route with a known turnaround: the first bench or one tree. Check the distance both ways. Walking, using a wheelchair or walker, and bringing a stroller are all ways to enjoy the same small outing. Leave room to exploreIf everyone wants more, add another section after checking its surface and slope. Keep the shorter plan available. More distance is an option, never the measure of a good day. A choice counts without spoken words.Offer two real options—“tree or water?”—using speech, familiar photos, objects, sign, or the person’s usual AAC. Keep “stop,” “more,” “quiet,” “help,” “toilet,” and “home” available. Give time to respond; if pointing is difficult, offer choices one at a time using their established yes/no signal. Honor refusal and changes of mind.For a blind or low-vision companion, offer brief descriptions and ask before guiding. For a deaf or hard-of-hearing companion, keep the plan visible, face them when communicating, and agree on a visual signal for stopping. Ask before touching anyone or moving their mobility equipment. 02 · An invitation, never a checklistEight ways to meet the season.Start with one appealing idea. Keep it, change it, or skip it. A quiet setting for one person may feel busy to another; there is no need to use every sense or turn the afternoon into a lesson. 01 SightNotice one gold leaf, a cloud, or a reflection from a comfortable position. Bring a leaf into view only where handling is permitted; a companion can describe its shape and color.Make it gentler: Try shade, a brimmed hat, or a still view instead of sparkling water. Looking away is fine. 02 SoundPause for wind in the trees, a bird, or leaves underfoot. If listening is not useful or enjoyable, watch branches sway or notice a bird’s movement instead.Make it gentler: Use preferred hearing protection and move away from roads, leaf blowers, barking, or crowds. No “quiet listening” performance required. 03 TouchOffer a permitted tactile exhibit or a familiar leaf from home on a tray within comfortable reach. Touch with a fingertip, through a glove, or not at all. Do not place objects in someone’s hand without agreement.Make it gentler: A favorite fabric or fidget can come along. Leave unfamiliar plants, fungi, and wildlife untouched. 04 SmellNotice the air near a pine grove, a garden, or the shore from the path. Let the person choose the distance; there is no need to pick, crush, or bring plants close to a face.Make it gentler: Skip scent activities around allergies, nausea, or aversion. Move away from strong smells; bring no added fragrance. 05 TasteHave a familiar snack or drink at a comfortable stopping place. An autumn picnic can mean the food someone already enjoys; trying a new flavor is entirely optional.Make it work: Follow the person’s usual eating and drinking supports. A non-food pause is equally welcome. Do not taste wild berries, mushrooms, leaves, or water. 06 Movement & balance (vestibular sense)Choose a short, smooth stretch at the person’s preferred speed, or stay still and watch the scenery. A turn or change in pace should be expected and agreed on.Make it gentler: Avoid surprise pushing, spinning, steep slopes, and uneven shortcuts. A stable seated position is a full way to participate. 07 Body position & effort (proprioception)Notice comfortable contact with a seat, backrest, or foot support. If already comfortable and chosen, carrying a light water bottle or moving along the path can offer another way to notice effort.Make it gentler: No added weights, forced stretches, or endurance goals. Rest and familiar positioning supports belong on the outing. 08 Inside-body cues (interoception)Offer a concrete choice: “drink or rest?” “jacket on or off?” Check comfort, temperature, energy, and toilet needs without requiring anyone to name a body sensation.Make it easier: Offer planned breaks and usual supports even without a request. Pause or leave when discomfort appears. 03 · Six states, a few good starting pointsWhere might you begin?These are researched planning ideas, not reports that our family has visited every location or audited access. Official information was checked October 14, 2026. Follow the links for current conditions, fees, and facilities; an “accessible” trail label does not describe every person’s experience. The surface is crushed stone and the path is five feet wide.Check the fit: Mass Audubon notes that portions can still feel steep or strenuous. Accessible restrooms and equipment loans are listed; confirm availability. The farmyard adds animal sounds, smells, and visitors.With a dog? Pet dogs are not permitted; service animals are welcome.Drumlin Farm access details & photo tour · Visitor rules New HampshireOdiorne Point State Park · RyeA small start: Ask staff about an accessible approach to a seaside picnic spot, or a short section of the paved recreation path along Route 1A. Try watching waves or noticing the sea air.Check the fit: The roadside route may bring traffic noise; natural-surface trails are different terrain. The park currently flags dune-restoration trail closures. Confirm the exact route, gate access, and seasonal restroom opening before setting out.With a dog? Pet dogs are not permitted.NH Parks trail access information · Odiorne conditions, map & visitor rules MaineWolfe’s Neck Woods · FreeportA small start: The White Pines Trail is identified as accessible in Maine’s park access guide. Begin at the second parking lot and choose a short out-and-back among the pines toward the bay views.Check the fit: Other park trails include uneven ground and steps. The rocky shore is a separate access question. Confirm the current White Pines surface, restroom availability, and seasonal conditions.With a dog? Park guidance allows leashed, attended pets under control; check current rules before bringing yours.Wolfe’s Neck Woods visitor information & map · Maine park access guide (PDF) VermontNorth Branch Nature Center · MontpelierA small start: A 0.3-mile Universal Access Trail loops around meadows and the community garden. The center lists compacted crushed stone, three benches, and a typical width of five feet, narrowing to three feet.Check the fit: The published maximum grade and cross-slope are each 6%; winter surfaces vary. Ask about toilet access when the center is closed. Try a bench stop to watch grasses move.With a dog? The center’s policy requires pets to be leashed; only service animals are permitted indoors.North Branch trail measurements & map · Center animal policy Rhode IslandClaire D. McIntosh Wildlife Refuge · BristolA small start: Audubon describes an accessible crushed-stone trail and wooden boardwalk through marsh habitat toward Narragansett Bay, with less than a mile of trails overall. Enjoy grasses, birds, or a short boardwalk section.Check the fit: Confirm boardwalk conditions and the distance from parking to your chosen stopping point. Bathrooms are available during nature-center hours; do not rely on access outside those hours. Coastal wind and wet boards may change the experience.With a dog? Pet dogs are prohibited.McIntosh Refuge access details & rules ConnecticutHammonasset Beach State Park · MadisonA small start: Choose a short section of the park’s paved-and-boardwalk coastal route. The full listed walk is 3.4 miles; there is no reason to complete it to enjoy the view.Check the fit: This is a popular shared route. Ask about quieter times, the nearest accessible parking and open restroom, and sand on the path. The summer beach-access mat is seasonal, so do not assume an autumn route onto the sand.With a dog? Leashed pets are allowed in picnic areas year-round; beach access has seasonal dates. Check the rules for the exact area you plan to use.Hammonasset routes & pet rules · Seasonal beach access information Pet rules and service-animal access are different. If you need a specific accommodation, ask the site directly. For an outing without a drive or admission fee, begin with a familiar sidewalk, public garden, or tree near home after checking its route and seating. 04 · A small plan to take alongBefore you go.Pick the details that matter to your group. A few minutes of preparation can leave more room for simply being there. Check the whole route. Parking or drop-off, surface, slope, width, steps, gates, seating, and the return journey—not just the trail name. Ask about wheelchair space beside benches and usable picnic-table clearance. Check the practical essentials. Open accessible toilets, any needed changing facilities, fees, pet rules, and current closures. In autumn, ask about wet leaves, mud, early closing, and hunting-season restrictions where relevant. Show what will happen. Use the person’s preferred format: a photo, spoken explanation, large-print note, or short visual plan. For example: “Arrive → choose a spot → pause → return.” Make the turnaround clear. Pack familiar supports. AAC and backup communication, water, usual food or feeding supplies, layers, preferred hearing protection, and the personal care or mobility equipment you already use. Keep essentials within reach. Agree on help and a way out. Ask what assistance is wanted. Plan for roads, water edges, and anyone who may need close support. Choose a nearby rest point and an easy return before anyone is tired. Let the day be enough. Offer breaks and “all done” throughout. No required touching, tasting, speaking, eye contact, posing, or finishing the trail. Watch, listen, rest, or head home together. One tree. One patch of sky. One very interesting smell, if you happen to be Ruby. There is plenty to begin with. More from the family albumA few more good days. title: A welcome before you walk through the door
summary: A thoughtfully welcoming toy shop in Bath, England: the story behind its autism-friendly sign, original watercolor illustrations and ideas to bring to our own Main Streets.
search: The journalGood ideas from farther afield My Small World · Bath, EnglandA welcome before you walk through the door.A little toy-shop sign, a place built around play, and a useful idea to bring home to our own Main Streets.An AUsome Life · October 8, 2026An imagined toy-shop welcome, inspired by the story. Original editorial illustration. A photograph of a sign outside My Small World, a toy shop in Bath, England, caught my eye. It announces that the shop is autism friendly. Then it gets to the part I especially like: what that means when you actually arrive. The sign offers to lower the music, soften the lighting and give people space. It reassures visitors about excited play, noise and moments of overwhelm. It invites families to say what would help. “Give you space to be you.”From My Small World’s welcome sign That is a lovely thing to encounter before you have even opened the door. The shop behind the signA whole little world of play. My Small World is an independent toy shop in Bath’s SouthGate shopping area. In the shop’s own account of its beginnings, the idea grew from a search for a special first-birthday present in 2003. That very personal starting point feels fitting for a business whose welcome has travelled so far beyond its front door. The team describes a shop with trees, changing seasonal foliage, birdsong and shelves of books, games, toys and things to make. Play is encouraged. The pleasure of looking, touching and discovering something is part of the visit they want to offer. There is a more recent chapter, too. Revo named My Small World its 2025 Independent Operator of the Year. The award’s description highlights the newer SouthGate store, its playful interior and a sensory space for neurodivergent families. That recognition helps put the much-shared sign in context: the welcome is part of a wider approach to the shop. The relief is in the details. When an ordinary errand takes planning, a specific welcome gives you something to work with. You can picture asking for the music to come down. You know that needing a little room is something the staff have already considered. One less conversation has to begin with an explanation. On its own website, My Small World explains that its team includes autistic people and parents of autistic children. The shop describes a commitment to helping families feel comfortable, grounded in that lived experience. What stays with me is the invitation to arrive as you are. There is room in that idea for a wonderful browse, a very brief visit, a pause, or deciding to try another day. Why it stays with usRoom for the day you are having. A toy shop can hold so much promise: something to turn over in your hands, a favorite subject on a bookshelf, the pleasure of choosing. For a family like ours, that invitation also needs room for an older child, an iPad used for communication and a visit that might be shorter than expected. The particular kindness of the sign is that the adjustments are offered before anyone has to ask. It makes room for a conversation about what would help today. A person can enjoy a lively display and still want the music lowered; someone else may prefer a quiet corner or a little more time. Familiar things within reach. Original editorial illustration. Bring that welcome to our own Main Streets. A bookshop, café, farm stand or hotel can make its welcome useful in the same way: tell people what help is actually available, and make it easy to ask. A few places to begin: Be specific about sound and light. Say whether music can be lowered, which areas are quieter, and what lighting can be adjusted. Offer time and space. Explain where someone can pause and whether they can step outside and return. Ask what helps before stepping in. Welcome different ways of communicating. Give people time to point, type, use picture cards or speak through an AAC device. Address the person directly and respect their answer. Keep the welcome age respectful. Autistic teenagers and adults belong in the picture, too. Offer help without assuming someone’s interests, abilities or preferred language. Those are ideas for other businesses to consider, beyond the adjustments described on this particular sign. The best version is a promise the staff understand and can keep.It can be as ordinary as telling a visitor, “We can lower the music. Would that help?” Then listening to the answer. A welcome has room for “yes,” “no,” “later,” and an answer given without speech. A small sign can start a conversation. For our family, the practical details belong right alongside the lovely ones. The invitation to look around matters. So does knowing that asking for a change will be met with understanding. I would love to see more of that on our own Main Streets: a clear, ordinary welcome, with enough detail to make walking through the door feel a little easier. If Bath is on your listStart with SouthGate’s current shop listing and My Small World’s contact page. The listings give different street numbers following the shop’s move, so confirm the entrance before setting out. The shop’s published telephone number is +44 (0)1225 312943.Ask what can be adjusted during your visit, how the sensory space works and whether there is a quieter time to come. Check the route into the shop, space to move around and nearby accessible toilets separately. A welcoming sign is helpful; each family will still have its own practical questions. About this noteThis is a reflection on a sign spotted online and the shop’s published approach, rather than a report from a family visit. The sign has circulated for years; we are sharing the idea, not announcing a new policy.Read My Small World’s story and autism-friendly approach or contact the shop before a visit. Shop information and the linked Revo award announcement checked October 8, 2026. Ask directly about the adjustments and access details that matter to you. title: The caregiver handover, made useful
summary: A practical caregiver handover with a short template, an arrival check, current-plan safeguards, privacy boundaries and a clear return of responsibility.
search: Put today’s plan first. A useful handover helps the next person act. Begin with today’s date, the agreed time together, what the person is expecting and anything that has changed. Keep the long history in its appropriate record. Make the plan with the person receiving support, using the communication they prefer and any assistance they need. Explain who is arriving, what is happening and how the visit will finish. Offer choices within the arrangements that are genuinely available. Before responsibility changes hands Confirm the incoming person has arrived and has agreed to take over.Review the important changes and invite questions.Check they can access the needed supplies, contacts and current instructions.Confirm what happens if plans change or the return is delayed. When support needs uninterrupted coverage, do not rely on an unanswered message as a completed handoff. Show how communication works today. Have the person’s usual communication tools available and ready to use, including a familiar backup if they have one. Show the incoming supporter where they are kept and explain any practical help needed to use them. Do not replace a familiar system with a new worksheet simply because the worksheet is convenient. Share the useful basics: how the person makes a choice, asks for help, signals a pause and indicates that they want to finish. If a signal is uncertain, say so. “This sometimes means a break; check with them” is more useful than presenting a guess as a fixed fact. The NJC Communication Bill of Rights supports meaningful choices, direct communication and access to working communication systems. The practical goal here is that the person can still participate when their usual supporter is away. Keep current care instructions alongside the short note. The handover is a summary of arrangements, not a substitute for the person’s current care, medical or emergency plans. Confirm that the incoming supporter is authorized, trained where necessary and able to provide the support being transferred. Give them access to the actual instructions and essential information they need, through the established private channel. Do not omit a critical safety detail merely to keep the summary to one page. Equally, do not improvise medication directions, eating or drinking instructions, lifting methods or emergency procedures in this template. If instructions conflict, are out of date or cannot be accessed, resolve the issue with the appropriate person before the affected activity or handoff. Follow the existing emergency arrangements for urgent situations. The short handover template. Use these headings in the private record or on the paper system you already use. The blank version is deliberately general. Add only the information appropriate for this recipient and setting; keep completed copies secure. Date and timePrepared: ______ · Support begins: ______ · Expected finish: ______ Today’s agreed planFirst: ______ · Then: ______ · The shorter version: ______ The person’s choicesWhat they have chosen: ______ · What is still open: ______ CommunicationTools and location: ______ · Useful partner guidance: ______ · Backup: ______ Food, drink and ordinary suppliesWhat is ready: ______ · Where the relevant current instructions are kept: ______ A pause or finishHow to check: ______ · Available place or option: ______ Changes that matter todayConfirmed changes: ______ · Question to resolve before handoff: ______ Current care and emergency instructionsPrivate location and version/date: ______ · Access checked: ______ Contacts and changes of planAgreed contact route: ______ · Backup route: ______ · Return-delay plan: ______ Responsibility acceptedOutgoing supporter: ______ · Incoming supporter: ______ · Time confirmed: ______ A completed handover can contain private information. Do not put it on a public noticeboard, leave it in a shared vehicle or paste it into an open online tool. Use the person’s agreed permissions and the provider’s requirements for storage and sharing. What a useful note sounds like. Illustrative example: “Today we agreed on the library and home. The shorter version is returning the books only. The communication bag is beside the coat and has been checked. Please confirm the current return time with me before I leave.” This example does not contain the safety instructions for a real person. Those still need to be accessible to the person providing support. Close the handover at the other end. Before leaving, give a brief factual update: what took place, what changed, anything needing attention and who has agreed to the next step. Complete required records in the proper system. Confirm that the next supporter has accepted responsibility where continuous support is needed. Revise the standing information when something changes.
